lines.text: In August 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait.

lines.text: Oil prices roughly doubled in a few months. Brent went from about $17 a barrel in July 1990 to above $40 in October.
lines.say: Oil prices roughly doubled in a few months. Brent went from about seventeen dollars a barrel in July nineteen ninety to above forty dollars in October.

lines.say: For India, which imported much of its oil, that hurt fast.

lines.text: India's oil import bill jumped by more than half in the 1990-91 fiscal year.
lines.say: India's oil import bill jumped by more than half in the nineteen ninety to ninety-one fiscal year.

lines.text: And the war hit a second wallet: money sent home by Indians working in the Gulf.
lines.say: And the war hit a second wallet: money sent home by Indians working in the Gulf.

lines.text: India airlifted more than 170,000 of its citizens out of Kuwait, in 488 flights over 59 days.
lines.say: India airlifted more than a hundred seventy thousand of its citizens out of Kuwait, in four hundred eighty-eight flights over fifty-nine days.

lines.text: It's still in the Guinness record books. But those workers' paychecks, and the dollars they sent home, stopped.
lines.say: It's still in the Guinness record books. But those workers' paychecks, and the dollars they sent home, stopped.

lines.text: So more dollars were flowing out for oil, and fewer were flowing in from workers.
lines.say: So more dollars were flowing out for oil, and fewer were flowing in from workers.

lines.text: Here's why that matters. A country pays for imports in dollars, not its own currency.
lines.say: Here's why that matters. A country pays for imports in dollars, not its own currency.

lines.text: Those dollars sit in a pile called foreign exchange reserves, at the central bank.
lines.say: Those dollars sit in a pile called foreign exchange reserves, at the central bank.

lines.text: In January 1991, India's pile was down to about $1.2 billion.
lines.say: In January nineteen ninety-one, India's pile was down to about one point two billion dollars.

lines.text: By June, it covered only about two weeks of imports. Lenders saw it, and new loans got hard to find.
lines.say: By June, it covered only about two weeks of imports. Lenders saw it, and new loans got hard to find.

lines.text: Politics added fog. In May 1991, during an election, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated.
lines.say: Politics added fog. In May nineteen ninety-one, during an election, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated.

lines.say: On June twenty-first, P V Narasimha Rao became prime minister, and he named an economist, Manmohan Singh, as finance minister.

lines.text: They walked into an empty vault. So what do you do when you run out of cash? You pawn the jewelry.

lines.say: Chapter two: gold on a plane.

lines.text: The first move came even before the new team took over.
lines.say: The first move came even before the new team took over.

lines.text: On May 16, 1991, the government leased 20 tonnes of seized gold to the State Bank of India.
lines.say: On May sixteenth, nineteen ninety-one, the government leased twenty tonnes of seized gold to the State Bank of India.

lines.text: That bank sold it to Union Bank of Switzerland, with an option to buy it back. It raised about $200 million.
lines.say: That bank sold it to Union Bank of Switzerland, with an option to buy it back. It raised about two hundred million dollars.

lines.text: That bought a little time. Not much.

lines.text: Then in July, the Reserve Bank of India pledged its own gold: 46.91 tonnes.
lines.say: Then in July, the Reserve Bank of India pledged its own gold: forty-six point nine one tonnes.

lines.text: It went to the Bank of England in four shipments, starting July 4, 1991, as collateral for a loan.
lines.say: It went to the Bank of England in four shipments, starting July fourth, nineteen ninety-one, as collateral for a loan.

lines.text: Chapter three: the rupee drops.
lines.say: Chapter three: the rupee drops.

lines.text: Back then, India's government managed the rupee's value. Today it's far more market-driven.

lines.text: On July 1, 1991, it cut the rupee's value. Two days later, on July 3, it cut again.
lines.say: On July first, nineteen ninety-one, it cut the rupee's value. Two days later, on July third, it cut again.

lines.text: Together, the rupee lost about 18.7% of its value against the dollar, by the central bank's own count.
lines.say: Together, the rupee lost about eighteen point seven percent of its value against the dollar, by the central bank's own count.

lines.text: Why do it in two steps? To test the reaction first. The second cut came after markets took the first one calmly.
lines.say: Why do it in two steps? To test the reaction first. The second cut came after markets took the first one calmly.

lines.text: Let's do the math on what a cut like that means.
lines.say: Let's do the math on what a cut like that means.

lines.text: If the rupee loses 18.7% of its dollar value, one rupee is now worth 0.813 of what it was.
lines.say: If the rupee loses eighteen point seven percent of its dollar value, one rupee is now worth zero point eight one three of what it was.

lines.text: So a dollar now costs 1 divided by 0.813, or about 1.23 times as many rupees.
lines.say: So a dollar now costs one divided by zero point eight one three, or about one point two three times as many rupees.

lines.text: Say an imported part cost 1,000 rupees before. After the cut, the same part costs about 1,230 rupees.
lines.say: Say an imported part cost one thousand rupees before. After the cut, the same part costs about one thousand two hundred thirty rupees.

lines.say: But flip it around. An Indian shirt or a software project suddenly looked cheaper to an American buyer.

lines.text: That's the trade-off of a weaker currency: buying from the world costs more, selling to it gets easier.

lines.text: A cheaper rupee alone wasn't going to save India, though. The rules had to change.

lines.say: Chapter four: the big rewrite.

lines.text: For decades, India ran on what people called the License Raj.
lines.say: For decades, India ran on what people called the License Raj.

post.title: In 1991, India flew 47 tonnes of gold to London. Here's why.
post.ig: In 1991, India flew 47 tonnes of gold to London to borrow dollars. Then it rewrote its economy.
post.tiktok: In 1991 India was two weeks from running out of dollars. So it flew its gold to London.
post.yt_desc:
In July 1991, India's central bank pledged 46.91 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England to borrow about $405 million, because its reserves could cover only about two weeks of imports. This video explains how the Gulf War oil shock and lost remittances drained India's dollars, why the rupee was cut by about 18.7% in two steps, and how the July 24, 1991 reforms ended most industrial licensing, cut tariffs and opened the door to foreign investment. Then we follow it to your wallet: generic drugs, Indian IT firms, US-India trade in 2025, and H-1B workers.
